title: The Kettle
passages:
The Marrow drew alongside the Kettle's low gate and Sol cut the engine. The sudden quiet left a hollow in the air, filled by the creak of lashed pallets and the slap of water against rotting hulls. The Kettle was the arcology's low gate, a warrens of docks where the waterline sucked at everything not tied down. Sol heaved the bow line over a bollard and made it fast, the rope biting into her palms.

Dey lay on the deck mat where she'd dropped him after the last dive. His chest rose in shallow, rattling pulls, each breath sounding like it was being dragged through gravel. His dive harness lay beside him, scrubber canister cracked open, useless. Sol had already stripped him out of his suit, but she couldn't strip the cold out of his lungs or the salt out of his eyes.

Pru Quill stepped over the gunwale, the berth book tucked under one arm. It was a heavy ledger, bound in leather gone stiff with salt, pages swollen at the edges. She didn't offer a greeting. She opened it to the current season and ran a finger down the column.

"Six berths left," Quill said. "That's all. Six names above the waterline before the storm bell shuts the channel for the season."

Sol leaned against the mast. "And if one of those six stays empty?"

"Then my own berth is forfeit," Quill said. "I don't get to shade the number. I can't lie. The book says six, I say six."

Dey coughed into his elbow, a wet, racking sound. He turned his head on the mat. "You came all the way out here to tell us you're desperate?"

"I came to name the price," Quill said. "That's my job. You wanted berths above the waterline. Here's the count. Take it, or the water takes you."

Sol glanced at Dey. His face was gray under the salt stubble, his lips blue at the corners. He was breathing faster now, shallow and fast, one hand clutching his side like he could hold his ribs together. "He's not cargo," Sol said. "He's crew."

"Then he's a name," Quill said. "Six names. Six crates of medicine. That's what the book wants."

A line snapped somewhere down the dock, and a salvaged trawler slammed against its mooring with a hollow thud. The wind shifted, bringing the smell of diesel and wet cordage. Sol pushed off the mast and knelt beside the mat.

"Six," Sol said quietly. "We can do six."

Quill closed the book with a dull thud. "The bell starts its count at the turn of the tide. You have until then."

She stepped back onto the dock, and the wood groaned under her weight. Sol looked down at Dey. His eyes were open, glassy, tracking her.

"You hear that?" Sol said. "Six berths. We're buying them all."

Dey managed a thin, wet laugh. "Of course you are. And who's the sixth name?"

Dey's question lands like a stone on wet wood. Quill doesn't look at him. She looks at Sol.

"The indenture," Quill says. "One name, bound to the Kettle until the debt works out. Yours, Dey Okafor. Six crates and your signature. That's the price for six berths."

Sol is on her feet before the last syllable. She steps between Quill and the mat, her body blocking the view, her hand coming up like she can cup Dey's ears shut. "Don't say it like he's here to hear it."

"I am here," Dey says. His voice is thin, rattling, but it carries. "Quit it, Sol. I'm not a child. Take your hand off my head."

Sol's fingers hover an inch above his salt-crusted hair. She doesn't touch him, but she doesn't step back either. "You're not signing anything."

"Someone has to," Dey says. "You want six names? I'm a name. I've been diving to buy back my freedom since I was sixteen, and now you're telling me the price is my freedom? That's rich."

"It's not freedom," Quill says. She can't soften it. She can't blink away the sharp edge. "It's an indenture. You work the debt off on the docks until the Factor's books balance. I don't set the terms. I just read them."

"You read them to my face," Dey says. "Why don't you just spit on me and get it over with?"

"Because spitting isn't in the berth book," Quill says. "Signing is."

Sol looks down at him. Dey's chest is heaving, each breath a wet scrap against his ribs, but his eyes are clear enough to cut. He grips the edge of the mat with one hand, knuckles white.

"You don't have to do this," Sol says.

"Someone does," Dey says. "Unless you've got six crates of medicine and a spare soul in your pocket. Hand me the pen, Quill. Let's see how the indenture reads."

Quill opens the book again. The pages are swollen, the ink dark. She holds out a stylus, the kind dock-wardens use to etch names into the leather so the salt can't wash them out.

Dey lifts his head from the mat. His breath whistles through his nose. "Go on," he says to Sol. "Cover my ears again. See if it changes the price."

Sol doesn't move. She looks at Quill, then at the stylus, then at Dey's face — gray, stubborn, alive.

"That's what I thought," Dey says.

The dock creaks. Somewhere on the frame, metal clamps into metal. The air feels like it's holding its breath.

Quill says, "Six crates. One name. The tide turns in forty minutes. That's all the time the book gives us."

Dey lets his head fall back onto the mat. "Forty minutes," he says. "Funny. That's almost enough time to change your mind."

Sol doesn't answer. She stares at the indenture line in the book, waiting to see whose hand will reach for it first.

The bell crew was already on the frame. Three dockhands in oilskins climbed the iron rungs without looking at the Marrow. One carried a padded mallet. The other two bore the striker arm, whalebone and steel, which had to seat in the cradle just right or the tone would choke and the count would fail.

Sol stayed where she was, between Quill and Dey, but she didn't raise her hand again. She could hear the berth book's leather creaking as Quill shifted her weight. Quill's stylus rested on the page, the tip already scored with a trial mark near the indenture line.

"Step back, Captain," Quill said. "The bell doesn't care whose hand reaches first."

"It should," Sol said. "It's counting names."

The first dockhand reached the top and dropped the mallet into the cradle. The bell hung above them, bronze and green with salt, bigger than a diver's helmet, its mouth turned down toward the water. The crew secured the striker, checked the line, and stood clear. Sol felt the vibration in the deck mat before she heard it.

Quill raised her free hand. "On the count."

The mallet fell.

The sound rolled, a low heavy boom that made the water under the dock shiver and Dey's ribs shudder under his skin. One. The number hung in the air, then died.

The dock went quiet. Not peaceful quiet. The kind of quiet that happens when everyone realizes they're holding their breath.

Dey turned his head on the mat. He looked up at the tarp overhead, at its ragged edge flapping against the frame, and he laughed. It was wet and broken, but it was a laugh.

"Of course," he said. "Of course it's me. Six berths, six crates, one indenture. They want the body that can't breathe and the name that's already signed. I'm the bargain-basement option, Sol. The one they want."

"They don't want you," Sol said. "They want six names above the waterline before the tide closes the channel."

"Then why am I the one who can't dive anymore?" Dey coughed, a racking thing that shook his chest. He spat salt into the bilge and turned his face back to Sol. His breath whistled through his nose. "Why am I the one with the cracked scrubber? Why am I the one lying here while you stand over me?"

"Because I'm still standing," Sol said. "Watch me."

She looked up at the bell frame. Five counts left before the channel sealed for the season.

Dey closed his eyes and laughed again, softer this time, up at the underside of the tarp where the salt stains ran. Of course the one they wanted was him.

Nia had been counting since the first strike and got six twice, and she didn't like either answer.

She sat with her back to the lashed crates, Teo wedged under her arm where the tarp dripped least. The crates were stenciled MERCY GENERAL PHARMACY on the side facing out, which meant the whole dock could read what the Marrow was carrying and nobody had to guess. Six of them. She had counted those too.

"Say my brother's name out of your book," Nia said.

Quill didn't look up from the page. "Vos, Teo. Age eight."

"And after that?"

"After that there's a column." Quill turned the ledger so the light caught it, which was as close to a kindness as she'd managed all morning. "Cargo class. Under twelve, no trade, no berth of his own. He rides with a name."

"Whose name?"

"Yours," Quill said. "You're the name. He's the weight."

"Great," Nia said. "I've been promoted to a boat."

Teo stirred and coughed, and she shifted him so his head was off the wet plank. His lips had that gray look again. She reached under the tarp to the cold-box, the hand-cranked cooler she'd been turning by herself for a year because asking a stranger to turn it meant telling a stranger what was inside, and put her palm flat on the lid. Cold. Good. Still cold.

Then she dug in her coat and came out with the log.

It was an oilcloth-covered tide almanac from before the water came, with eleven blank pages sewn into the back using gut and a sail needle. No slate could reach it. Nothing could reach it. No wire, no dock, no warden with a stylus, no voice on a bell. She uncorked the pen — a real pen, brass, squid ink, stolen off a drowned desk in the tower where she'd found Teo — because pencil smudges and she was done writing things that smudge.

She wrote: *Bell struck once. Tide turns in forty minutes.*

She wrote: *Six crates. One Dey. Six names.*

She wrote, because Quill had said it and Quill could not shade a figure: *Price for six berths above the waterline, spoken by the dock-warden to Captain Sol Ferreira's face.*

"Write that I said something clever," Dey said from the mat.

"I write what happened," Nia said. "Not what you wish happened."

"Then write that I laughed."

She wrote that he laughed at the underside of the tarp. It was true, and it took up a line, and the line was his.

"What's an indenture?" Teo asked. His voice was a scrape under the bell's ring.

"It means somebody else owns your hours," Nia said.

"You own mine," Teo said.

Nia put the pen down and got the lid of the cold-box open and checked the ampoule rack by feel, two rows of six, all present, and shut it again. "Drink your water," she said, which was not an answer, and he was eight, so it worked.

At the bow, Wren had her kit roll open on the deck and was rebuilding her harness for a dive nobody had ordered yet. She did that. Nia had watched her do it twice already: check the rig while your hands still remember the shape of it. She had the twin spools out of the housing — two wire reels side by side, one recording while the other took the slack, so a diver's slate gets the whole descent and not just the pretty part — and she was thumbing the take-up tension with her eyes somewhere else entirely. The pony bottle, the little backup cylinder a diver carries at the hip for the last few minutes when the main line runs dry, sat uncapped beside her knee. The reader's shears were in her coat pocket, where she kept them now instead of in the roll.

"Wren," Nia said. "How many times has it rung?"

Wren's hands kept moving. "It's rung," she said.

"That's not a number."

"No," Wren said. "It isn't."

The mallet fell again. Two. The note went out flat across the water and came back off the arcology's flank a half-second later, thinner.

Nia wrote the time. Quill's stylus scored another trial mark near the indenture line, and Dey watched her do it, breathing in those short wet pulls, and didn't say anything at all.

Wren wiped her palms on her thighs, stood, and crossed the deck to where her harness hung on the frame stanchion. She went down on one knee in front of it, the way she always did, and reached for the chest strap.

Her fingers closed on empty webbing. The clip where the spit can should sit— the hard-shell drop-box a diver jettisons so the crew still gets his record if he doesn't surface— was bare metal and frayed thread.

Wren patted her thighs, her coat pockets, the deck beside the harness. Nothing. She lifted her slate—the recorder that kept a diver's descent on wire so the crew had a record if they didn't surface—and checked the screen.

A red beacon icon pulsed beside a depth readout: forty-two meters. Six hours and fourteen minutes of battery remained on a transmitter she had never armed.

The spit can was down there. Calling up from the same shelf where Ivo Salas had waited fourteen months in an air pocket, breathing air he couldn't afford to waste.

"I don't do forty-two," Wren said. "I don't dive uncommanded. I don't lose gear."

The bell boomed again. Three. The sound shook the lanterns on the frame and turned the water under the dock dark and choppy. She tapped the screen. The ping came steady, one every few seconds, a countdown she hadn't started.

She had never been below thirty meters on this boat. She had never gone down alone. She had never left gear behind. Her hands remembered every clip, every strap, every weight she'd ever clipped in. This clip had been closed when she came aboard. She had checked it before Sol cut the engine.

Unless she hadn't. Unless she had cut it loose, slipped over the side, and dropped forty-two meters into the dark while the Marrow sat at the gate, then climbed back up and forgotten the whole thing.

"That's not how it works," she said. "I would remember."

Would she? Below a certain depth in the towers, people started losing memory, and it never came back. Forty-two meters was well past that depth. But the spit can wasn't a person. It was a box. It didn't lose anything. It just kept blinking.

Wren stood too fast and knocked her knee against the stanchion. She didn't curse. She stared at the slate, at the red dot marking forty-two meters, at the battery ticking down under the tolling bell.

Forty-two meters stopped being a place on a chart and started being a bill someone had already come to collect.

The mallet fell again. Four.

She needed Sol. She needed to say something before Dey signed anything, before the tide turned, before the battery died and took whatever the can had recorded with it.
